questions.question: Explain fully why the tropics are heated more strongly than the polar regions, even though insolation arrives at the top of the atmosphere at the same rate above both.
questions.expected_answer: Insolation reaches the top of the atmosphere at roughly 1 367 watts per square metre everywhere, so the difference is created by the earth's curvature and the angle of incidence. Near the equator the midday sun is close to overhead, so a beam of a given cross-section lands on a small patch of ground and energy per square metre is high; poleward the surface leans away and the identical beam is smeared over a much larger, oblique area. Angle also controls path length: an oblique polar ray slants through several times the thickness of atmosphere that a vertical tropical ray crosses, so far more of it is scattered, reflected and absorbed before it lands. Albedo then widens the gap, because fresh snow and ice reflect roughly 80 to 90 per cent of what they receive while the dark tropical ocean reflects under 10 per cent. The three effects reinforce one another, which is why the difference is a permanent feature and not a seasonal accident.

questions.question: Using Cape Town at 34 degrees south, show with calculation how the axial tilt and revolution produce a summer and a winter, and explain why 'the earth is further from the sun in winter' is not an acceptable answer.
questions.expected_answer: The axis is tilted 23,5 degrees from the vertical and keeps that lean fixed in direction (parallelism) while the earth revolves once every 365 and a quarter days, so the overhead sun migrates between 23,5 degrees north and 23,5 degrees south. Midday solar altitude equals 90 degrees minus the angular distance between the place and the overhead sun. On 22 December the declination is 23,5 degrees south, so the angular distance is 34 minus 23,5 equals 10,5 degrees and the altitude is 79,5 degrees. On 21 June the declination is 23,5 degrees north, so the angular distance is 34 plus 23,5 equals 57,5 degrees and the altitude is 32,5 degrees. That 47-degree swing is reinforced by day length, which falls from about fourteen and a half hours in December to under ten in June — weaker energy for fewer hours. The distance explanation fails because the earth is in fact closest to the sun in early January, which is southern summer but northern deep winter; one distance cannot produce opposite seasons in the two hemispheres, so the tilt must be the cause.

questions.question: Describe the global energy surplus and deficit, explain why poleward transfer must occur, and name the processes and carriers that achieve it.
questions.expected_answer: Comparing absorbed shortwave radiation with longwave radiation lost to space at each latitude shows a permanent surplus between roughly 40 degrees north and 40 degrees south and a permanent deficit poleward of about 40 degrees in each hemisphere. If those imbalances went uncorrected the tropics would heat without limit and the poles cool without limit, yet the equator-to-pole temperature difference stays broadly stable from decade to decade, so energy must be transported poleward continuously and on a very large scale. The atmosphere does roughly three-quarters of the work through the tri-cellular circulation, the mid-latitude westerlies and their travelling depressions, the jet streams, and above all latent heat carried inside water vapour and released on condensation — about 2,5 megajoules for every kilogram of water. Ocean currents do the remaining quarter; South Africa shows both limbs, with the warm Agulhas Current carrying tropical heat south along the east coast and the cold Benguela Current drawing polar water north along the west coast. Averaged over the whole planet and over years, energy in equals energy out, so any change to albedo or to greenhouse gas concentrations forces the temperature to shift until balance is restored.
